items.reason: Trading the strong d4-bishop is valid, but the c6-knight never blocked the c8-bishop. It misses Re8+ and Qxb6.
Rg8 does hit the queen with tempo, but a rook on g8 doesn't guard e4; d5 already does.
Nd7 retreats without tempo, and e6 is Black's own pawn. It also invites Bxh7+ sacrifices.
Ne4 hits the f6 bishop, not e6. Black owns the queenside majority, and no pawn is down.
e7 is Black's own pawn, so there is no tempo. A knight on c6 does not guard c7, which is empty anyway.
Winning the queen is correct; the knight recapture develops, and from d7 it attacks e5 alongside Bg7.
Bg3 rescues the bishop from g5xh4, but the best line leaves White an isolated d-pawn, so pawns aren't healthy.
Black's pin and pressure on c3 are real. Castling unpins the king and gets it out of the centre, though c3 still falls.
Nxd5 removes the knight hitting e7 and f6, parrying the threat. The idea misses the follow-up Bxf5 winning back the pawn.
A knight on f8 covers h7, not g7. Guarding h7 against Bd3/queen ideas is still a real defensive motive.
g2 is defended by the king and Qd2. Qxg2+ simply loses the queen for a pawn; Black gains no material.
Bxe4 trades for the d5-defended e4 knight, not c6, and it isn't free. The muddled plan ignores Nxc4.
d5 does threaten Nc6, but it needn't be taken: Na5 also parries. Capturing is still best.
Bxb3 captures, not recaptures. A bishop on b3 doesn't guard a3. Queens aren't relevant; Nxe5 was best.
Nxe5 rightly regains the pawn, but g7 is Black's own pawn. White's queen takes it; Black cannot attack it.
The e4 knight is Black's most active piece. Capturing it after dxe4 Qxe4 wins a pawn, though the player doesn't mention that.
Bd7 neither attacks e5 nor guards d6. Its real point is breaking the c6 pin, threatening Nxe5.
cxd4 removes White's d4xc5 pressure and undoubles Black's pawns; 'freeing the queen' is vague but not false.
Nf3 saves the knight but doesn't guard a2, and White is down material, not ahead.
No a4–d2 diagonal exists; Qg5 stops guarding c3 and hangs the queen to Qxg5.
Capturing the checking bishop is right, but Nc6 is impossible afterward; neither knight can reach c6.
Winning the g3 bishop is the real point, but Qh5 does not attack Black's king on e7.
No black knight sits on e7; that's the bishop. Bxg5 also misses winning 1...Nd4, which is far stronger.
The b3 knight attacks White's queen on d2. Capturing it is forced and equalizes; Qe1 is worse.
The b4 knight doesn't guard b6. After Bxb4, Black recaptures with the bishop, so there's no tempo on the queen.
Black's king is already on g8, so castling is impossible. dxe5 opens the d-file, leaving Bd3 hanging to Qxd3.
Qb7 does cover c7 and hit b2, but b2 was already attacked and c5 is left hanging.
No bishop sits on c7 or attacks the queen. d6 blocks Bf4's diagonal to c7 rather than guarding c7.
Black has no extra pawn; White is up material. Bb4 pins and wins the queen, which the idea misses.
Qg6 does not attack h3, which the g2 king defends. The real point is pinning the Ng5 block and winning it.
Nf3 doesn't attack the b7-bishop; it blocks the long diagonal, shielding h1. That defence is the real point.
Be7 attacks nothing, so there is no tempo. It allows Bxf6 and Nd5; Nbd7 is better.
Ne8 rescues the attacked f6-knight and opens the g7-bishop, adding pressure on e5. 'Not by running' is loose wording.
The h4 pawn attacks g3, not the queen. It is rook-defended. gxh4 wins a pawn but wrecks structure; Nxh4 is better.
White is down two pawns, not up material, and there is no open h-file to use; cxd4 was best.
Qa5+ is check, but e1 holds White's king, not a pawn; material is equal, so nothing to give back.
The d5 pawn doesn't attack Black's king; exd5 is right because it regains material and frees Black's development.
dxc5 doesn't open the c-file; White's c4 pawn remains and the queen is on d8. It also ignores Re8xe4.
d3 holds White's bishop, not a knight. Queens come off after ...Qh4 anyway, so neither claim fits the move.
Qh5 doesn't block any a-pawn or protect Nc3, which falls in the line. Its point is threatening Qh7 mate.
White is down material and cannot castle; Ne5 doesn't block e4 and allows Nxe5 dxe5 Qxd1.
Winning the undefended queen is correct, but no white knight is under attack, so 'it is lost' is false.
dxc5 lets Black recapture Bxc5+ with check, activating the bishop. It neither clears a rook's path nor stops queenside play.
gxf3 exf3 just restores Black's f3 pawn while exposing White's king to ...Qxh3 and Qg2 threats.
1...e4 attacks the f3 knight with tempo and moves the attacked e5 pawn to safety. This is the engine's best move.
Castling is impossible since Black's king is on b8, and material is equal, so there's no extra material.
Qf2+ checks, but White's f4 pawn blocks the f-file to f5. It forks neither queen nor rook.
Qf4 recaptures on c1 along the f4-c1 diagonal. Black just trades queen for rook, gaining nothing.
The b4 pawn neither attacks c3 nor defends e3; Re3 attacks the queen. Qxb4 also loses ground to Qc7.
Rfc8 does not attack the a5 knight; it only takes the c-file. Meanwhile b7 simply falls.
d3 does attack Be2, but Black has no a-file presence. It ignores Bxa2 and lets White play Ra8+.
f6-bishop is defended by Qf7 and Nd7. Qg7+ is a queen sacrifice: hxg7 then Rh8+ promotes and mates.
Bb3 gains no tempo (e6 is defended) and doesn't guard c3; it leaves d1, allowing ...Rd1+.
Ne7 saves the knight but attacks d5, not h5; there's no attack on White's king.
White isn't down a piece, only a pawn. Taking e5 opens nothing toward g7, since White's own f6 pawn blocks that diagonal.
Material is equal, so White isn't 'winning back' anything. Still, removing the knight that hits d4 and h4 is relevant.
The knight goes to h6, not h7. Nh6 gains no tempo and forks no rooks; it only saves the knight.
fxg4 removes the knight threatening h2 and the Ne3 fork, regaining material; it's the engine's best.
Material is equal and g2 is captured, not won back; Kxg2 wins the bishop for a pawn.
The king is on g1, not the e-file. Kh2 escapes Rd1's back-rank check; the queen guarding h2 is irrelevant.
The d4 knight wasn't attacked, and Black has no material to win back. On e6 the knight hangs to Rxe6.
Bd3 does not guard the queen on d5; Bb7xd5 simply wins it. Qd4 was needed.
Ng7+ does check and saves the attacked f5 knight, but Be2# mates at once.
The king is on g8 and in check on the g-file, not the e-file. The idea misses escaping check.
Bxc1 wins the checking rook, but the bishop on c1 guards neither f3 nor the d8 queen.
Qh7+ doesn't attack b8, and Nf8xh7 wins the queen. White's queen wasn't loose; Qg3 is best.
b4 does kick the queen, but material is equal: there's no extra pawn and nothing to win back. Real plan: c5 passer.
Rxd5 captures Black's only bishop; Black has no bishop pair. The real point is winning material and defusing threats.
Nd2 forks the b3 queen and f1 rook; the engine line continues with O-O-O, keeping Black's extra pawn.
Ra6 stays on the a-file and does not defend d5. The queen isn't attacked anyway; Nxf7 wins.
h7 isn't undefended: Qe7 guards it. After Qxh7+ Qxh7 Bxh7 Kxh7, White loses a bishop for a pawn.
The e7 rook neither guards d6 nor White's king. Bxe7 simply wins a rook; Nxb5 was stronger.
Black's king on d8 has no castling rights; Rxb5 also leaves the h8 rook to Bxh8.
Rf8 does attack the bishop with tempo, but it simply retreats. 1...e6 first traps it.
Qd4 does guard e5, but it doesn't block the pawn; it misses the trade offer and the threats on c4/b2.
Kd8 escapes check and guards e7, but Kf8 also does; the d-file king allows Bd5 and Rd1.
Rg3+ forks nothing, d3 is White's own pawn, and Qxg3 simply captures the rook.
It is no fork: the queens attack each other, so 2.Qxe5+ follows. The real point is trading queens to stop mating threats.
Rb8 moves the f8 rook onto the open b-file, not off it, and does not guard c4.
A knight on d4 cannot attack d2, and it unpins the c-file: Rxc8+ Rxc8, Rxc8+ wins a rook.
Neither black rook is attacked, and d2 is Black's own pawn. Rf1 actually offers the rook to Rxf1.
Re1 is checking the king, not attacking c2 (Rc1 does). It isn't free: Rxe1+ recaptures, winning the exchange.
c5 does hit the queen, but Black is already up material; there's nothing to win back.
Bxe2 is a capture, not a recapture. It doesn't affect the kingside pawns and ignores White's Bd5 and checks.
Correct: f5 is undefended, so exf5 regains the pawn for free. This is the engine's best move.
Rxc1 removes Black's rook, takes the open c-file and stops Rxe1+. It omits the main point: winning a rook.
Guarding h7 against Rxh7# is right, but g8 lies on a2-g8, not a2-h7. Qg8 stops the mate.
Nd4+ checks and hits undefended c6, but Rb8 is unguarded and Bc7 still attacks it.
King is on g1, not the e-file; Kf2 escapes Bh2+ but doesn't guard h2, and queen can't reach h3.
Qb3+ is check, but Rxb3 simply wins the queen. No queen trade happens; g3 was best.
Qb3+ gives check but doesn't attack the f4 knight, which e5 defends. It also abandons pressure on d3.
Ng3 neither attacks e6 nor guards c3; its real point is Nh5+ hitting f6.
Rd1+ checks but attacks nothing on a7; no double attack exists. The rook claim is meaningless.
Nc6 covers d8/e7 and enables Nc7#; bxc6 removes it, parries the mate and saves the rook.
The d6 bishop is indeed undefended, but nothing attacks a queen: White has none, and Bxd6 doesn't hit b6.
Rg8+ checks but forks nothing; the rook doesn't attack e5. The engine prefers g4, preparing Rg8+ with mate.
f6 does attack g5, but it doesn't hit d4. It actually blocks the g7-bishop's diagonal to d4 and weakens the king.
Rxd8 trades away the d6 rook itself, so it isn't kept. It also misses the winning 1.c4.
Bxd5 captures the d5-knight itself, no guarding knight exists; after cxd5 there's no c6-pawn to attack.
O-O-O is legal and unpins the e7-bishop from the e-file, so it really defends f6.
